text_blocks.snippet: Herpes outbreaks are triggered by the reactivation of the herpes simplex virus (HSV), which can lie dormant in nerve cells for extended periods. Several factors can cause this reactivation, including stress, illness, hormonal changes, and physical trauma.
snippet_highlighted_words: the reactivation of the herpes simplex virus (HSV)

list.snippet: Both physical and emotional stress can weaken the immune system, making it easier for the virus to reactivate.
Stress hormones, like cortisol, can also play a role in triggering outbreaks.
When the body is fighting off an infection, the immune system is busy, which can allow the herpes virus to reactivate.
Any illness that weakens the immune system can potentially trigger an outbreak.
Fluctuations in hormone levels, particularly during menstruation, can be a trigger for some individuals.
Any injury to the skin, including cuts, sunburn, or even minor irritation, can provide an entry point for the virus to reactivate.

list.title: Fatigue:
list.snippet: Extreme tiredness can weaken the immune system and increase the risk of an outbreak.

list.title: Sun Exposure:
list.snippet: Excessive sun exposure, especially around the lips, can irritate the skin and trigger oral herpes outbreaks.

list.title: Medications:
list.snippet: Certain medications that suppress the immune system can also trigger outbreaks.

list.title: Suppressed Immune System:
list.snippet: A weakened immune system, whether due to illness or other factors, can make it easier for the virus to reactivate.
